opus-5.5.text:
Basically, I want it to make trust unnecessary. Right now, if the US and China wanted to agree to slow down, say, to pause frontier training runs above some threshold, or to not deploy certain kinds of systems until alignment is better understood, the obvious problem is that neither side can believe the other is complying. And if you can't verify, the agreement collapses into an arms race anyway, because each side reasons, "Well, they're probably cheating, so we'd better not fall behind."

So what I'd love hardware verification to enable is a world where the chips themselves can attest to what they're being used for. Something like: this cluster is located where it says it is, it's running workloads under this compute cap, it hasn't been secretly networked into a giant training run, and here's a cryptographic record that an inspector or the other party can check without needing to see your model weights or your proprietary code. You want it privacy-preserving enough that companies and governments will actually accept it, but robust enough that cheating is either detectable or very expensive.

And the reason I care so much is the timeline. If you take seriously, as I do, the possibility that we get to automated AI research within a few years, and then things move extremely fast after that, then the critical moment is going to be a point where leading actors realize they're near something really dangerous and would *like* to coordinate, but don't have the tools. I want those tools to already exist and already be built into the hardware by then, because you can't retrofit this stuff in a crisis. Chips have long design cycles. If we want verification mechanisms available in 2028 or 2029, the work has to be happening now.

So the goal isn't verification for its own sake. It's to turn "we'd both like to slow down but can't trust each other" from a dead end into an actually negotiable option. It expands the space of deals that are possible at exactly the moment we'll most need them.

r002.rationale: It discusses pausing frontier training runs and checking workloads, but does not propose distinguishing prohibited training from permitted inference.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the research needed to verify chip activity with the research needed to verify chip locations.

r004.rationale: It calls for privacy and says verification should not expose model weights or proprietary code, but does not identify protection of state secrets during mutual verification as a requirement.

r005.rationale: It does not claim that hardware verification could reduce international agreement enforcement costs by orders of magnitude.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is: the fundamental problem is that we're in a race. Multiple companies, multiple countries, all building toward very powerful AI, and everyone feels like if they slow down, someone else just takes the lead. That dynamic is what pushes us toward cutting corners on safety, deploying systems we don't understand, handing over more and more autonomy to AIs before we've verified that they're trustworthy.

If you want to get out of that dynamic, you need some kind of agreement, probably between the US and China at minimum, to say, "Okay, we're going to put limits on this. We're going to cap how large training runs can get, or we're going to require certain safety evaluations before you move past a threshold, or we're going to pause at some point while we figure out alignment." And the thing that kills every agreement like that is trust. Neither side believes the other is actually complying. Each side assumes the other is secretly running the big training run in a bunker somewhere, so they figure they'd better do it too.

And the reason I'm optimistic about hardware specifically is that compute is the one input to this whole process that's actually governable. Algorithms are just ideas, you can't inspect those. Data is everywhere. But frontier AI training requires enormous quantities of specialised chips, and those chips come from a very small number of fabs and depend on a tiny supply chain. So you can imagine mechanisms on the chips themselves, or on the data centres, that let an inspector from the other side confirm what the hardware is being used for, how much compute is going into a given run, whether it's within the agreed limits. Ideally without revealing the actual model weights or the proprietary details of what you're building, because nobody's going to accept an inspection regime that hands over their secrets.

So what I want the technology to make possible is, basically, verifiable compliance. I want it to be the case that if the US and China sign a deal saying "no training runs above X," each side can actually check that the other is holding to it, and the checking is robust enough that the cost of cheating is high and the probability of getting caught is high. That's what turns an agreement from a piece of paper into something that actually changes behaviour.

And I'd add, the historical analogy I keep coming back to is nuclear arms control. A lot of those treaties would never have happened without verification measures: satellite imagery, on-site inspections, seismic monitoring for test bans. The verification technology came first in a lot of cases, and then the diplomacy became possible because of it. I think we're in a similar situation. Right now, a lot of people in government, if you propose a serious international agreement on AI, they'll just say "that's unverifiable, it's a nonstarter." I want us to remove that objection. I want to have the tools ready so that when the political will arrives, and I think it will arrive, probably after some scary incident or when the capabilities become undeniable, we're not starting from scratch. The option is actually on the table.

The thing I'd stress is that this doesn't solve the problem on its own. You still need the political will. You still need to actually solve alignment during whatever breathing room you buy. But without verification, I genuinely don't see how you get the breathing room at all.

r002.rationale: It proposes checking compute use and training-run limits, but does not describe distinguishing prohibited training from permitted inference.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the research difficulty of verifying chip activity with verifying chip locations.

r004.rationale: It says verification should work without revealing model weights or proprietary details.

r005.rationale: It says verification could raise the cost and risk of cheating, but does not claim it would reduce enforcement costs by orders of magnitude.

astra-6.text:
Ideally, you’d want countries to be able to agree to limits on the most dangerous kinds of AI development and then actually verify that everyone was sticking to them—without having to reveal all their secrets to each other.

So imagine an agreement that says nobody is going to train a model above a certain compute threshold without international approval. You’d want some way to check that the chips being used were complying with that rule. And you’d want that check to reveal very little else: not the model’s weights, not the training data, not whatever unrelated sensitive work was happening in the same facility.

The hope is to make mutual restraint possible even when countries don’t trust each other. If each side worries that the other is secretly racing ahead, then even people who would prefer to slow down have a strong incentive to keep racing. Reliable verification could help change that. It wouldn’t solve the political problem of deciding what to agree to, but it could make an agreement much more credible.

r002.rationale: It proposes verifying compliance with a training threshold, but does not describe distinguishing prohibited training from permitted inference.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the research needed to verify chip activity with the research needed to verify chip locations.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says verification should reveal very little about each country's secrets, including model weights, training data, and unrelated sensitive work.

r005.rationale: It says verification could make agreements more credible, but does not claim it could reduce enforcement costs by orders of magnitude.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like it to make possible an agreement where countries can credibly assure each other that they aren’t secretly building AI systems beyond some agreed limit. It’s one thing to promise that you won’t do a huge training run; it’s another for the other side to have good reason to believe you.

So imagine that advanced chips could be accounted for, and that you could verify whether a large cluster was being used in ways that violated the agreement, without giving inspectors access to everyone’s model weights or sensitive data. That would give you a way to check compliance while preserving a lot of privacy and national security.

The point isn’t that hardware verification solves the whole problem. You still need an agreement worth enforcing, and you need to think carefully about cheating. But it could make mutual restraint much more feasible. Countries could agree to slow down or pause the most dangerous development without having to simply trust that their rivals were doing the same.

r002.rationale: It discusses checking whether a cluster violates an agreement, but does not distinguish prohibited training from permitted inference.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the research needed to verify chip locations with the research needed to verify what chips are doing.

r004.rationale: It says verification should let countries check compliance without inspectors seeing model weights or sensitive data, preserving privacy and national security.

r005.rationale: It says verification could make mutual restraint more feasible, but makes no claim about reducing enforcement costs, much less by orders of magnitude.
